chapter: Louis Armstrong, Gene Krupa and the drum school
title: Taking Sid Catlett's place in Louis Armstrong's All Stars

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Well I guess we've come to the point where you went with Louie Armstrong. Spring of 1949.... Let's talk about that.

Okay. Well, see, when Joe Glaser first got that group together, the All Stars, see they called me first before Sid Catlett but I was busy then with my own little group and doing record dates and things around and I just didn't want that gig then to go out on the road. Then I didn't know how the quintet was going to go. And so they got Sid Catlett and the next thing I heard, oh goodness, after the group was about one week old, well

they were a sensation. Sid Catlett, Jack Teagarden, Earl Hines, Barney Bigard, and Louie, they were sensational. And Sid, the group, Velma Middleton singing, and that group just worked and worked and worked until Sid was-took ill, sick, then they couldn't go on the road any more. Sid and I were real tight and when they called me again for the gig I wasn't sure whether Sid was sick or not, but I had Sid's number, I called Sid at his home, they were in New York. I said "Joe Glaser has been calling me and wants me to come over there with Louie. Now are you sick and can't you make it out on the road any more, because I don't believe them, I want it to come from the horse's mouth. I mean are you leaving the group? Because if you're leaving, I'll come in there and take the job." He said, "Yeah, Cozy, I'm leaving." So that's how I took the job and we opened in, where was it, Detroit, forget the name of the club with no rehearsal or nothing, and that's my first time ever playing every night Dixieland. I'd been listening to Louie and loved his playing, and loved Dixieland, but never actually sit down and just play all those different tunes--"Muskrat Ramble," "That's A Plenty" and all those things, you know, so many different Dixieland tunes, and so there's certain little beats that fit a lot of them too, you know, that I wasn't acquainted with. But after you listen to them for a while, and then you can get them because you've heard them before

on records. So when I went in the drums were sitting right up front, and Barney and Jack were standing right next to me and so we're about to open and Louie, "Hey, Cozy how you doing?" All right, Louie you know, and I figured that some time during that time he'd say well, Cozy, we're going to do this, we're going to play this, we're going to play this." So I asked Barney, I said "Barney, what are we playing?" I said, "Louie hasn't said anything to me," and Barney said, "Man, don't pay Louie any mind, because Louie ain't going to tell you nothing." So Louie just looked at me and said, "Cozy, man, we don't have time to just say a lot of things up there, just cock your ear and straight ahead," and that's what I did for about a couple of weeks until I learned all the tunes, and it was peaches from then on. It was just wonderful, we never rehearsed, and I was with him five years.
